newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital market closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital market closing report.

text.p: Ignoring uncertainty about the outcome of the French election, 10-year bond futures erased most of their losses to settle just inside negative territory, supported by strong domestic liquidity, dealers said.

June PIBOR closed higher after dealers said it was oversold on Wednesday but one analyst said she believed the three-month June PIBOR interest rate future risked a "pretty strong correction" on Monday if the left wins Sunday's runoff vote.
A survey by Reuter conducted on Thursday said a victory by the left would knock another 30 basis points off June PIBOR.

But economists believed the long term impact would be limited. The median forecast for June PIBOR after a win for the left was 95.95, implying three-month rates of 4.05 percent, compared with 96.27 on Thursday, despite the fact more and more people are betting on a change of government.
But by October 15, the 12 economists surveyed predicted the PIBOR future would recover to 96.38 if the left won, or 96.65 if the centre-right coalition retained power.
The franc would rally two centimes if the right pulled off a late recovery and slide to 3.40 per mark if the opposition left held onto its first round lead, the survey suggested.
The franc strengthened on Thursday to trade at 3.3785, up from its three-month low of 3.3828 on Wednesday.
Analysts said that the bond market had been helped by short-covering and options expiry as well as domestic liquidity.
The 10-year bond future fell in morning trade on non-resident selling but then was helped by domestic buying.
"We keep seeing domestic buyers on each downturn, that's why the market is holding up so well," said analyst Nathalie Filet of Paribas.
"But I think that tomorrow people will be pretty cautious and if anything, the tone will be a bit bearish," she said. "I don't think the market is sufficiently prepared for a left victory."
The market was swept by rumours of conflicting private opinion polls about the outcome of next Sunday's final runoff vote. The left scored an unexpected win in the first round.
The cash market outperformed Germany slightly with the negative yield spread on French 10-year bonds against their German counterparts widening to minus 10 from minus nine.

One economist at a major French bank said the Bundesbank's stinging attack on the German government over its plans to revalue the nation's gold reserves to qualify for a single currency made him fearful about prospects for monetary union.
"For the first time since 1992, I am worried about the project. Not that I am saying it won't go ahead but I feel there's a very, very strong risk," he said.
He added France's new apparent willingness to insist that Italy be a member added to his apprehensions as he said German public opinion might not be able to accept Italy joining.

Ex-cabinet minister and centre-right campaign spokesman Nicholas Sarkozy said it was important to have as many countries as possible in the first wave of monetary union, including southern countries such as Italy.

He also said there was consensus among the centre-right that a single currency should not be delayed because of failure to cut deficits to exactly 3.0 percent of gross domestic product, the target in the Maastricht treaty.
Earlier this week, Prime Minister Alain Juppe said it was "obvious a second decimal point will be interpreted with intelligence and not using rigorous accounting methods."
The recent statements by the centre-right have brought it closer to the positions of the Socialists.
-- Penny MacRae, Paris Newsroom +33 1 4221 5452
